posts.content_md: I’ve seen dot matrix holograms that produce 2D images that are both grayscale and rainbow-coloured depending on the viewing angle. How is this achieved? posts.topic_title: New to holography and dot matrix holograms. I have a few questions.
posts.author: Din
posts.post_subject: New to holography and dot matrix holograms. I have a few questions.
posts.content_md:
I think I was the first person to use a dot matrix machine at American Banknote Holographics in 1994; since that was 30 years ago, I haven't any idea how they've progressed since then. However, based on my knowldege from 1994:

If you make a hologram with just two beams - no object, just two beams - you get what's called a 'grating'. If you make such a hologram on material such as photoresist, then such a hologram will give you a colour based on the illumination angle - as you turn the hologram you'll see different colours. In a dot matrix machine, a single unexpanded beam is sent down a tube. At the end of the tube is a beam splitter, splitting the beam into two beams, one beam continuing down the tube, and the other coming off at right angles to a mirror and being redirected. Where the two beams meet, there is a photoresist plate (see diagram below). The tube can be rotated, so the plane of the two beams is also rotated. The rotation angle of the tube - the plane of the two beams - is determined by some digital image, back in 1994 it was Photoshop. What basically happens (happened?) is the angle was set by the digital pixel value, and the digital pixel value was set by the colour on the digital image. So, for example, the pixel value for orange in the RGB colour space is R = 107, G = 80, B = 0; this particular pixel value would rotate the tube to a specific angle and record a single 'dot/pixel' on the hologram. If this particular dot/pixel on the hologram is viewed by a light source at the specific angle, it would appear orange. If viewed by a light source at any other angle, it would change colour.

The photoresist plate is set on an X-Y translation stage. In the machine I worked on in 1994, the first dot/pixel recorded is the top left pixel on the digital image. The tube was rotated to whatever the value of the first pixel on the digital image was, a shutter opened, and the first dot/pixel was recorded on the resist plate. Then the plate was translated along the X direction (sideways), the tube was rotated according to the pixel value on the next pixel in the digital image, and the next dot was recorded. This process continued - shifting the plate along the X direction, rotating the tube, and exposing, until the last pixel on the first line in the digital image was recorded. Then the plate went back to the zero position in X, and incremented in the Y, and the machine would start on the next line of pixels on the digital image. As the machine scanned the digital image as a raster, the hologram dots were recorded as a raster, with different planes of the two beams. If you viewed the hologram from any specific light source, all the recorded pixels in the raster would show a different colour because the tube - and hence the plane of recording - was different for each recorded dot. 

The reason you see rainbow colours is that the recording plane is rotated, so the direction of the reference is altered for each pixel - note the angle between ref and object is set by the side mirror (45 deg in the 1994 machine) but the direction is varied. Now, given any illumination source, the different directions of the recorded dots will show up in difrferent colours - each dot appears as a different colour; remember that all directions will diffract in a resist hologram. Not sure why you see a greyscale image, I can only speculate that you're reconstructing with a very diffuse source, which will give you a grey-ish image. Another possibility is that the "grey" image is not a diffracted image but burn-in, when the dot/grating was burnt into the material by over-developing.

I don't think there are any significant changes since 1994. It's possible the software can pick up any image from any imaging software, ie it's not limited to just Photoshop as it was back then.

posts.content_md:
Very interesting. Thanks! I have a few questions.

1.) In the photoshop stage, you would design the image with the colours that you would want to appear on the dot matrix hologram? 

2.) So, the tube rotating changes the azimuth angle of the beams, which affects the angle of the grooves on the photoresist? But what about the groove spacing (pitch)? As far as I understand, the groove spacing in a diffraction grating is what controls the color, and the groove angle is what controls the angle at which that color appears.

As for the grayscale image, the dot matrix hologram I’m referring to is on the Canadian bill. At some angles, you see the portrait of a former prime minister in grayscale; at others, the same portrait is coloured (turquoise, dark blue, orange, and more depending on the angle). The grayscale is not printed or burned - it’s also revealed through diffraction.

posts.post_subject: New to holography and dot matrix holograms. I have a few questions.
posts.content_md:
> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Wed Aug 06, 2025 1:13 pm:** In the photoshop stage, you would design the image with the colours that you would want to appear on the dot matrix hologram?

To some extent at American Banknote Holographics (ABNH). The Marketing division at ABNH would procure an image from some customer, and pass the image idea to the Art Dept. The Art Dept. would then create the Photoshop image, with some collaboration with the Dot Matrix operator (me). Together, myself and Art would try and figure out what colurs in Photoshop would create what effects in the dot matrix. Then, I'd load the image and make a dot matrix on a reject resist plate (one that's low quality). Art and Marketing would look at it, then determine changes to make the customer happy; this would go through about 3 or 4 iterations. Finally, I'd record the dot matrix on a high quality resist plate and sent it to Production, who'd transfer it to a flexible foil. If the customer approved, Production would finally transfer it to a card or plastic.

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Wed Aug 06, 2025 1:13 pm:** So, the tube rotating changes the azimuth angle of the beams, which affects the angle of the grooves on the photoresist? But what about the groove spacing (pitch)? As far as I understand, the groove spacing in a diffraction grating is what controls the color, and the groove angle is what controls the angle at which that color appears.

You're right that the groove spacing controls the colour. But, the groove spacing in a dot matrix is fixed by the mirror/beamsplitter combination, so the interbeam angle, which determines the spacing, is fixed at 45 deg. (for the one I used). However, in a dot matrix, the direction of the two beams controls the colour. As the azimuthal angle is varied, the interbeam angle is always 45 deg but the direction of the "off-normal" beam, the beam coming off the mirror, changes direction. So, if we arbitrarily assign directions of, say, North (N), East (E), South (S) and West (W), then, for example, a specific pixel value of the Photoshop image may twist the splitter/mirror (SM) combination to N, another pixel value may twist the SM combination to some angle between N and E, and still another pixel value may twist the SM combination to S. In all of these cases, the SM combination always impinges light at 45 deg but from different directions. This has the effect of causing a glittering, varying look to the image is rotated and as each dot, referenced at 45 deg but from a different direction, is referenced at the right direction. Some dots come in at certain directions, and, as the hologram is rotated, different dots come in. Since this is a thin/surface hologram, as the hologram is rotated, colours fade in and out as the hologram is rotated; they don't 'wink out' as the hologram is rotated.

You can see the effect on a You Tube video I found. We actually took a video of an actual dot matrix I made in 1996, but can't attach it. I'm assuming you can't attach a video. 

Anyway: [https://www.youtube.com/shorts/BuGHf1iGHFs](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/BuGHf1iGHFs)

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Wed Aug 06, 2025 1:13 pm:** As for the grayscale image, the dot matrix hologram I’m referring to is on the Canadian bill. At some angles, you see the portrait of a former prime minister in grayscale; at others, the same portrait is coloured (turquoise, dark blue, orange, and more depending on the angle). The grayscale is not printed or burned - it’s also revealed through diffraction.

I didn't know the context, that's it's on your currency bills. In this case, the 'greyscale' hologram is multiplexed onto the dot matrix hologram.

There is a form of hologram, variously called 'open aperture' or 'achromat' (there's a running joke in holography that every hologram has about 6 ways to describe it!). In this form of hologram, there's only one reference angle from one direction, and the image has to be viewed at the reference angle. But, the image is grey scale, or 'achromatic', ie without colour. Multiplexing refers to the idea of exposing two or more holograms on the same medium. In your case, the dot matrix hologram is exposed, then the achromat is exposed, then the entire plate with the two multiplexed images is processed so as to show a single hologram(s). You can see an example of an achromat we made when I worked at Icon Holographics in London about 1983 for a well-known beer company.

 I also took a look at some of your notes and you have a Fourier Transform (FT) hologram of a maple leaf. When a single point source, such as Christmas tree lights, is viewed through the FT hologram, there appears a maple leaf surrounding the light source.

posts.content_md:
> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 07, 2025 6:29 pm:** Okay, I think I’m starting to get it. Just to be clear:The beam that goes straight down the beam splitter always has the same position. The beam that is split toward the mirror always comes down onto the substrate at a 45 degree angle, but its azimuth position can be changed by rotating the tube. Groove spacing is fixed, but colour can still be controlled by changing the groove angle.

Yes.

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 07, 2025 6:29 pm:** P.S. Because groove spacing is fixed, I’m guessing your limited to the colour range produced by that fixed spacing

In those days, Photoshop had a 24-bit colour depth - eight each for R,G and B, which amounted to about 17,000 colour values which had to cover 360 degrees of twist, meaning about 47 colour values per degree.

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 07, 2025 6:29 pm:** Since this was 30 years ago, how complex would it be to DIY a similar laser setup today?

The basic principle is pretty simple. You send a laser beam into a tube with a beamsplitter and attached mirror (the *attached* mirror is important because this fixes the groove spacing). In our case, the laser was sent horizontally to a mirror that diverted it downwards, ie the beam was diverted to be vertical. This vertical beam was sent into a rotating tube with a platform to hold the beamsplitter, a mirror attached to the platform diverting part of the beam so as to meet the straight through beam at 45 deg.and a hole in the platform to allow the through beam to access a plate. The tube was connected to a stepper motor which was controlled by software. The software "took in" a pixel value from Photoshop, and sent that information to the stepper motor. The stepper motor then rotated the tube through some angle determined by the software. The tricky part is beam alignment and the software. You'd have to access the colour buffer where the bit values for the colour of a specific bit was stored, then send this to the stepper motor controller, where the controller would have a look-up table for angle vs bit value. In our case, the software was written by a student from a local college. If memory serves, the software was written in Pascal. Today, probably writing in C++ may be easier. It may even be possible to have AI write it (Fair disclosure, I'm not a great fan of AI). Also, back then the process was slow, for a 4x4 in (~10cm x 10cm) image, I'd start it on Friday and let it run all weekend; sometimes, it was still running on Monday morning. Today, with more powerful lasers and better stepper motors, it could probably run a lot faster. However, modern imaging software today has up to 32-bit colour, making over a million colour values, which would be tricky for a maximum twist of 360 deg.

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 07, 2025 6:29 pm:** I looked into it a bit. It seems like grayscale achromatic holograms require higher-level equipment like an electron beam. Does that sound right?

No, it's made in the conventional process. First, a hologram is made by exposing a plate by a laser to an object/transparency about 8 inches from the plate. This hologram is viewable only in laser light, and is traditionally called an "H1". This H1 is then set to project the image in space, and a second hologram plate is placed in the (projected) image area, this traditionally called the "H2" and is viewable in ordinary light. At this point, the direction and method of reference beam determines what kind of hologram it becomes. If the reference for the H2 comes in from the other side of the H1, the hologram is a reflection hologram. If the reference comes in from the same side as the H2 it's now a transmission H2. If you illuminate the H1 with a single slit of laser light, the transmission H2 reconstructs in bands of colour, called a "rainbow hologram". If the geometry is a transmission geometry, and there's no slit on the H1, you get an achromat.

Here's a good explanation from Alec Jeong of Integraf - my primary source for holographic materials: [https://www.integraf.com/resources/arti ... -holograms](https://www.integraf.com/resources/articles/a-simple-holography-easiest-way-to-make-holograms)

posts.content_md:
> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Fri Aug 08, 2025 2:19 pm:** I’m more so referring to the limitation of a fixed groove spacing. If the groove spacing is fixed, doesn’t that mean that the only colours you can get on the dot matrix hologram are whatever diffracted colours you get from that fixed groove spacing? You can change the angle at which those colours appear, but it would still be those colours? How many total colours is that?

The hologram is a surface/thin hologram, so you get a large range of diffracted colours. The hologram is dispersive, therefore all wavelengths in the source light would disperse. The exact colours, and the exact range vs angle of viewing depends on the exact value of dispersion, which in turn, depends on the way the original was processed, and the surface quality of the bill. In the ABNH dot matrix, we used a He CD laser at a wavelength of 457nm, with an interbeam angle of 45 deg., which gave a spatial frequency (grooves per millimetre) of sin(45)/0.000457 ~ 1094 l/mm. If the bill couldn't take that frequency - which I suspect it can't, you'd lose some dispersion, and therefore some range of colours. For example, dvd's have a groove spacing of 0.74 microns, and so a spatial frequency of ~ 1351 l/mm. If you hold up a dvd to a light source and twist or turn it, you'll see the same (ish) effect as a dot matrix hologram - a range of colours that depend on the angle of viewing, despite a fixed spatial frequency. But, a dvd has a groove depth of 0.14 microns, whereas a resist hologram has, typically, a groove depth of about a micron - so the dispersion of the dot matrix is higher on the plate. But, when it's transferred to paper, you'll lose some spatial frequency and groove depth, which limits the dispersion.

In your second picture, the portrait looks like an achromat, and the spire below looks like a dot matrix. But I'd have to hold a bill to be more precise.

posts.content_md:
Hi,

I'll try to step in.

As Dinesh pointed out somewhere, it is close to impossible to guess how a specific DOVID (diffractive optically variable image device) works based just on low resolution photographs/videos with unknown illumination. I did not inspect $50 Canadian bill, but perhaps someone in my neighbourhood might have one so I could take a look then.

I am not sure what is your primary interest, Jay. Would you like to know how the Canadian bill DOVID works, or how to make something similar using dot matrix? 

To explain: A DOVID can be made using variety of mastering technologies, for instance conventional holographic setups, a dot matrix machine, image matrix optical lithography, single pixel optical lithography or e-beam lithography (to name a few). Moreover, you can use for instance an image matrix system and make a DOVID that looks like a dot matrix DOVID even on a microstructure level. I have no reason to assume that the DOVID on the Canadian bill has anything to do with dot matrix. So, if you are interested how the Canadian bill works, it may be completely misleading to start with an assumption it is a dot matrix origination.

It would be also good, Jay, if we knew what is your level of understanding holography and optics and why do you want to know. You may be, for instance, a teacher of physical optics who knows holography just theoretically and would like to know some practical aspects. Or, perhaps you don't know anything about holography or wave optics and you would like to build a dot matrix machine as a hobby project. Or anything else. It is easier to explain something when one knows the level of the guy who is asking.

Petr

posts.content_md:
That's much better. 

Is there any particular reason why you photographed the rainbow colors on the obverse side, while the grayscale on the revese side?

If I were inspecting such a hologram, I would fix the note and make it perfectly flat (use a new note, tape it to a flat surface) and fix the position of the camera (a tripod) so that it points to the note at normal incidence. Then I would take a point light source (cell phone flashlight is fine) and move it to the left and right off the camera, and upwards and downwards off the camera. This could be done manually. If one has access to a machine able to move something, one can make photographs of the note when the light is positioned in a grid of locations. One can read a lot of information from such photographs.

Dou you have an access to an optical microscope? For instance, school or hobby microscopes may be fine. One can easily see the overall structure of the DOVID. For instance, a dot matrix hologram is composed of small "dots", size typically tens of micrometers. Each dot then contains parallell strips (a grating) of pitch that might be difficult to recognize using a cheap microscope (below 1 um). But the overall structure, the "dots", should be easily visible even with the cheapest equipment.

When looking at the grayscale portrait: is it always a positive image, or it turns negative under some circumstances (black becomes white and vice versa). That would help to guess the idea how it was made.

To your point "...if diffraction inherently splits light into spectral colours": this is not entirely correct. A diffraction grating of suitable pitch and depth causes color dispersion, that's right. But when the grating pitch is coarse, color dispersion may become unnoticeable. On the other hand, when the pitch is very fine (below wavelength), the grating does not make diffraction orders (simply said) and color dispersion does not appear as well. Moreover, such a fine grating may absorb light and make so called "diffractive black". Also, a relief that is not as regular as a grating, for instance random noise, the reflection is mostly achromatic; this is sometimes called "diffractive white". The portrait could be, for instance, created by many small dots, some of them regular gratings making the rainbow effect and some of them diffractive blacks or whites to make the grayscale effect. But this is just a vague idea how such a thing could be done; I have no reason to assume that the $50 note is done like that.

Petr

posts.author: lobaz
posts.post_subject: New to holography and dot matrix holograms. I have a few questions.
posts.content_md:
That microphotograph definitely looks like a conventional printing screen. I think there is no reason to assume that the grayscale portrait is treated on the diffractive structure level; it is more likely created using other technology. 

One could indeed print that portrait using conventional technologies. If it was black ink, then I doubt you would see negative image in transmission, as black ink absorbs light in both reflection and transmission regime.

Another option might be to attack the reflective layer. To explain: the base of the window with the DOVID is transparent. If you apply a diffractive structure onto it, it would work mainly in transmission, its effect in reflection is very weak. To improve the behaviour in reflection, one applies a metallic layer on top on the structure, for instance a thin layer of aluminium. If you intentionally corrupt the aluminium layer, reflectivity is lost and the spot may look darker than the unaffected neighbourhood.

Yet another option would be to attack the transparent base itself, for instance using strong laser pulse, and burn it locally. That would make the base black throughout the volume. This approach, however, would unlikely lead to a negative image in transmission, I'm just noting that to show there are various techniques employed in security printing. (By the way, such laser heat treatment is used to personalise ID cards, driver licenses etc.)

If you want to learn more about methods used in security printing, check the book Optical Document Security by Robert L. van Renesse.

To your dot-matrix related question. I think this is now a mere academic excersise, I don't think the grayscale image is done on a microstructure level (although I cannot exclude that). Anyway: a conventional dot matrix machine, as described by Dinesh elsewhere, is not designed to do such things. But a skilled operator might introduce e.g. diffusers into the optical path to expose noise-like patterns to get diffractive white, or to expose many gratings in a single dot to achieve a similar effect. I have never worked with a dot matrix machine, perhaps Dinesh could comment. I don't think you can easily create subwavelength gratings to achieve diffractive black with a dot matrix approach. In any case, you create individual dots (conventional holopixels, special pixels) sude by side.

posts.content_md:
> **lobazwrote:↑Thu Aug 28, 2025 12:53 am:** Anyway: a conventional dot matrix machine, as described by Dinesh elsewhere, is not designed to do such things. But a skilled operator might introduce e.g. diffusers into the optical path to expose noise-like patterns to get diffractive white, or to expose many gratings in a single dot to achieve a similar effect. I have never worked with a dot matrix machine, perhaps Dinesh could comment. I don't think you can easily create subwavelength gratings to achieve diffractive black with a dot matrix approach. In any case, you create individual dots (conventional holopixels, special pixels) sude by side.

It's unlikely that a conventional holographic dot matrix would have some sort of diffusive structure overlaid on the gratings. This would imply that the diffusion would carry over to the next "dot", exposing it photographically. If a grating were recorded on top of an already (photographically) exposed area, the modulation would decrease. The result would be some sort of "dot matrix speckle", where the diferent dots would vary in efficiency, and the higher efficiency dots would have a high contrast against the lower efficiency dots. I doubt there would be the smooth transition that you see with dot matrix images. 

As for exposing many gratings in a single dot, this is possible if more than one mirror is used (see my previous explanation as to where the single mirror is fixed). However, over and above the problems of alignment of several mirrors and one beamsplitter, you would have cross-talk in any one grating. If this cross-talk spilt over to the next grating, you would see several diffraction patterns.

As I've said (for the fourth? fifth? time now), given any visual effect, there are a variety of ways of accomplishing this; Petr has given several ways of producing the given effect. To find out how this particular effect *was actually* created, you'd have to examine one in your hands, under a variety of reconstruction geometries. Otherwise, you end up going through a plethora of speculation - finally ending up in a never-ending rabbit hole of speculation. Even if two or more people could actually examine one on hand, there may well be different speculations. I've come across this several times before, when two or more holographers were asked "How was this done?". I was asked to examine a Magic Leap headset, along with other holographers, and we all came to different (but not too different) conclusions.

At the end of the day, isn't it the point of security holograms to confound analysis, even by professionals? The idea of security holograms is to make it (very) difficult to actually determine how it was done, even by holographers. I remember around 1983 - 1984, when ABNH was boasting that it's embossed rainbow holograms could not be compromised. Jeff Blyth proceeded to contact copy a visa dove (I think) that sent the entire security holography community into a panic. Jeff, from Cambridge UK, got a week's holiday at a swank New York hotel, all paid for by ABNH, to explain how he did it.

posts.content_md:
> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 28, 2025 1:35 pm:** I’ve had talks with someone in the Optics subreddit. According to them, holopixels with multiple high spatial frequencies can cause grayscale in the far field depending on the viewing angle.

Not sure what that means. In fact, not sure what a 'holopixel' is, since in conventional digital displays, the appearance of pixels are independant of any specific illumination source.

The far field diffraction pattern of any aperture is the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern, which in turn, is the Fourier transform of the aperture function. If the aperture is a sinusoidally varying spatial function, whatever the spatial frequency, then the Fourier transform, and hence the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern, is a Dirac function, or rather three Dirac functions.(Yes, Petr, I know the Dirac function is srtrictly not a function - you criticised me on this many years ago over some comment I made to Kaveh; the Dirac function is really a distribution or a functional ). I can't understand the far field Fraunhofer pattern "greyscale".

> **JayFritoeswrote:↑Thu Aug 28, 2025 1:35 pm:** And if direct laser writing were used, he says, allowing for lines with wavy edges, both spectral colours and grayscale could form in the far field.

Once more, don't know what "direct laser writing" is. But, again, the far field pattern is a Fourier transform of the aperture function.

It is vitally important to understand that a hologram, in and of itself, is not a hologram, it's a variation of spatial and phase properties on, or in, some structure, such as a thin grating or a Bragg structure. It becomes a hologram if - and only if - it is illuminated by some source with a specific spectral profile and direction. Displaying a "hologram" in a picture or video with no inormation as to the illuminant gives almost no information. Thus simply showing a picture, or video, of a "hologram" without any illuminant information, and asking how the visual effect could be created is an excercise in rhetoric .

Most display/security holograms and/or gratings are designed to display/reconstruct a specific image or an optical effect with a specific illumnation source. If the hologram is not illuminated in the way it was designed to be, the image/optical effect will not reconstruct in the way it was designed to reconstruct.

posts.content_md:
As for "diffractive white" and "diffractive black": hard to tell if there are other ways to name it. Security holography is a very niche business, the insiders do not reveal details too much and finally, the business is drowned out by marketing jargon - every company makes its own terms to differentiate from competition. I don't think there are any "standard" names for it, I'm just used to these terms. At lest "diffractive black" could be searched as zero order devices or zero order DOVIDs, or as structural colors.

Mostly the same applies to the term "holopixel". If you are in a niche of dot matrix, then perhaps it is a common term there, I don't know. I am used to talk about dots and hogels. By a dot I mean a spot with a simple grating within. By a hogel I mean a basic structural element of a certain type of hologram; a hogel is typically composed of several dots. But I don't think such terms are widely accepted, it is always necessary to define terms when starting discussion. I am not surprised Dinesh "does not know what a holopixel is" -- he has been in holography for a couple of decades and has seen how various terms emerge, disappear, change their meaning or are used differently in different applications.

As for how grayscale is done: I fully agree with Dinesh that it's just a rhetoric excersise without detailed examination of the hologram. If you are really interested, try asking someone with a decent optical microscope if you can look at $50 note (try the nearest high school). Observe the hologram both in small and big magnifications. In small ones, such as 20x, try observing the overall structure and try to spot regular properties. In big magnifications such as 100x, use a high numerical aperture lenses, such as 0.95, and observe the details of the microstructure. Moreover, as 100x lenses have very shallow depth of focus, try scanning through the volume of the film to see whether everything is located in a microstructure or if there are several layers or even volume features.

It is also very instructive to build a simple analysis device. Put the hologram on a flat surface such as a table. Take a sheet of translucent plastic or paper sheet, make a small hole in it and position it a few inches above the hologram, parallel to the table. Then take a laser pointer, position it above the hole in the sheet so that it sends the light beam downwards through the hole to the hologram. There it reflects from the hologram and diffracted light hits the translucent sheet. You can then observe from above where is the highest light concentration. Such a simple device helps you to analyse various places on the hologram. When there is a simple diffraction grating on the hologram, you should clearly see sharp diffraction orders on the translucent sheet; you can even reveal orientation and pitch of the grating from the analysis of the orders. When there is a diffractive white, you should see a large blurry spot on the translucent sheet. If you use a near-UV laser pointer (405 nm), it is sometimes possible to check whether high frequency gratings are present.
